items.label: section_header
items.text: ELECTROLYSIS AND REDOX

items.label: text
items.text: You will learn more about oxidation and reduction reactions in Chapter 14. Oxidation and reduction are words used to describe what is happening to things in certain chemical reactions. We can define oxidation and reduction as follows:

items.label: list_item
items.text: Oxidation occurs when something loses electrons.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Reduction occurs when something gains electrons.

items.label: text
items.text: We usually simply shorten this to oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons. A way of remembering this is the mnemonic OILRIG.

items.label: text
items.text: If we look again at the electrode equations in the electrolysis of lead(Il) bromide, we see that the lead(Il) ions gain electrons at the cathode:

items.label: formula
items.text: P b ^ { 2 + } + 2 e ^ { - } \rightarrow P b

items.label: text
items.text: Gain of electrons is reduction. The lead(Ill) ions are reduced to lead atoms.

items.label: text
items.text: The bromide ions lose electrons at the anode:

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 B r \rightarrow B r _ { 2 } + 2 e \bar { r }

items.label: text
items.text: Loss of electrons is oxidation. Bromide ions are oxidised to bromine molecules.

items.label: text
items.text: If something loses electrons something else must gain electrons and so oxidation and reduction always occur at the same time: we talk about redox reactions, red(uction)ox(idation). In the reactions going on at the electrodes each equation only shows one of the processes occurring, either oxidation or reduction, and so we call these half-equations. Both these reactions involve ions and so, in the exam, you may be asked to write ionic half-equations representing the reactions at the electrodes.
